stories.title: Larkspur
passages: Nora Fitch read the review three times before she believed it. The critic had called Larkspur "the most assured debut kitchen the city has seen in a decade," and by nine that morning the reservation line had rung so often that Dee finally took it off the hook. Regulars who used to slide in on a Tuesday now found nothing open until the following month. A local television crew wanted to film the pass during service. Nora walked the dining room before the doors opened, running her thumb along the edge of tables she and her sister had sanded themselves eighteen months earlier, and felt the particular lightness of watching something improbable become solid. Their produce supplier called just to say congratulations. An investor who had turned them down for their first loan sent flowers with a card suggesting lunch. That night the room filled by six and stayed full past eleven, plates going out in a rhythm that felt less like work than music, and when the last table finally left, Nora and Dee stood in the empty dining room and laughed until they had to sit down on the floor, giddy, too happy to clean up right away.

By late spring the reservation line had calmed to something Nora Fitch could manage without help. Most nights Larkspur ran three-quarters full, which the accountant said was healthy, though Nora still glanced at the empty four-tops near the window and did the math out of habit. Her fish supplier had switched trucks and the deliveries now arrived erratically, sometimes at ten, sometimes not until noon, so she had learned to build the day's specials around whatever showed up intact. One line cook quit without notice to move to his girlfriend's city, which meant Dee picked up knife work three nights a week between managing the front. A regular complained on a review site that the room was too loud, and another posted that it was the best meal of her year; Nora read both between rolling silverware. She renewed the lease for another two years, a decision that felt neither bold nor risky, just necessary. In the evenings she sometimes stood at the pass and thought the restaurant felt less like a miracle now and more like a job, which was, she supposed, exactly what it was meant to become.

Nora Fitch spent most of March doing math that refused to come out right. Two of the walk-in's compressors had failed within a week of each other, and the repair bill alone ate the cushion she had been saving for new chairs. The health inspector's visit, usually a formality, turned up a cracked tile behind the dish pit that needed replacing before he would sign off, which meant closing the kitchen for two days she could not afford to lose. Dee had started coming in late, tired and short-tempered, and when Nora asked why, her sister only said she was "handling things," which was not an answer. A supplier called to say their credit terms were changing from thirty days to cash on delivery, effective immediately, after a payment had gone out late. Bookings for the coming weeks were thinner than they had been since the opening month, and Nora caught herself hoping a slow Tuesday meant people were saving up for the weekend rather than staying away entirely. She lay awake calculating whether payroll would clear before the compressor invoice did, and for the first time in over a year, it did not feel obvious that it would.

The fire started in the exhaust hood a little after midnight, long after the last plate had gone out, and by the time the alarm company reached Nora Fitch she was already watching the orange light against her bedroom ceiling from a text her neighbor had sent. She arrived to find two engines blocking the street and smoke still rolling out where the front window had been. A firefighter had to hold her back from the door. Somewhere inside were the reservation books, the walk-in full of a week's ordered inventory, the pass she and Dee had sanded themselves, all of it now black water and ruined plaster. Dee arrived barefoot, having run the six blocks from her apartment, and the two of them stood on the opposite curb in the cold not speaking, because there was nothing yet to say. A fire marshal told her it would be days before anyone could go inside, and that the wiring behind the hood looked old enough to be part of the problem. Nora thought of the twenty tickets already printed for the following night's private party and understood, standing there, that she would have to call every one of those people herself.

Three weeks after the fire, the insurance adjuster's letter arrived, and Nora Fitch read it standing in the parking lot because she could not make herself wait until she got home. The policy excluded damage traced to wiring that had not met code, and the fire marshal's report had used exactly that word, code, twice. Without the payout, the lease's remaining eighteen months became a debt with no asset behind it, and the landlord's lawyer had already sent a letter of his own. Dee stopped answering calls that week, and when Nora finally reached her, her sister said flatly that she had warned her about the hood inspection back in March and that Nora had said there was not money for it, which was true, and hearing it said back to her in that voice was its own kind of burn. The bank froze further disbursement on the equipment loan pending review. Nora sat at her kitchen table surrounded by folders she did not have the heart to sort and understood that she had lost not only the restaurant but very possibly her sister, her savings, and the small apartment she had put up as partial collateral, all in the space of a month she could barely remember living through.

By August, Nora Fitch had taken a job on the line at a chain steakhouse near the highway, the kind of place with laminated menus and a walk-in stocked from a central warehouse, and she told herself it was fine because a paycheck was a paycheck. The manager was twenty-six and had never run a service in his life, but he signed her timesheet, and that was what mattered now. She was renting a single room from a former server of hers, having let the apartment go rather than fight the bank over it, and most nights she came home too tired to do more than eat standing at the counter. Dee still was not speaking to her, though a mutual friend mentioned she had taken a job managing another restaurant across town. One evening, an old regular from Larkspur recognized her under the fluorescent lights, said how sorry he had been to hear the news, and left his card with a note asking her to call if she ever wanted to cook something that was actually hers again. She put the card in her wallet rather than her pocket, which she understood, folding her apron that night, was its own small decision to keep it.

The stall Nora Fitch rented at the Saturday market was really just a tent and two folding tables, but by October she had worked out a menu of four dishes she could hold at temperature for six hours without either dish tasting like it had been sitting. Some Saturdays she sold out by noon; others she stood in the rain and packed up half her inventory to give away rather than waste it. The market fee ate more of the margin than she liked, and the generator she rented for the induction burners was unreliable enough that she had learned to have a backup plan for cold plating. She had not called the man who gave her his card, not yet, though she carried it in her wallet still, now soft at the corners. Dee had texted once, a short message about their mother's birthday, and Nora had answered in kind, nothing more. She was saving what she could into an envelope taped inside a cabinet, still short of what she would need for even the smallest lease, but the number was, for the first time since the fire, moving in the right direction instead of the wrong one.

A photograph of Nora Fitch's braised short rib, taken by a stranger at the Saturday market, was shared enough times that by the following weekend a line had formed before she had finished setting up the tent. A food writer for the city paper came through unannounced and asked for her name twice to make sure he had spelled it right. Orders came in faster than her two folding tables could plate them, and for the first time since Larkspur she had to turn people away not because something had gone wrong but because she had sold out. A produce wholesaler she recognized from her old accounts offered her thirty-day credit without being asked, saying he had heard she was cooking again and wanted in early. She hired a teenager from the neighborhood to help with the register so she could keep both hands on the pans. That night, packing up under string lights with her feet aching in a way that felt almost pleasant, Nora allowed herself to imagine, for the first time in nearly a year, a room with a door on it and her name above that door, and the thought did not feel foolish the way it would have even a month before.

The lease Nora Fitch signed in November was for a space a third the size of Larkspur, a former sandwich shop two blocks from the market with a kitchen just large enough to turn around in, and she thought it was the most beautiful piece of paper she had ever put her name to. The small-business loan had come through faster than the loan officer said was typical, helped along, he admitted, by a folder of press clippings about the market stall. Dee called the same week, and though the conversation started stiffly, it ended with her sister asking, quietly, whether there might be room for her at the new place, front of house, same as before. Nora said yes before Dee finished the sentence. They met at the empty storefront that weekend and stood in the bare room sketching where the bar would go, where the two four-tops would fit by the window, and for an hour neither of them mentioned the fire at all, which felt, to Nora, like its own kind of forgiveness, or at least a down payment on one.

Renovations on the new place, which Nora Fitch and Dee had taken to calling Larkspur Two before they had settled on a real name, were running eleven days behind because the electrician kept getting pulled onto bigger jobs. The health inspector's preliminary walk-through had gone fine except for a note about the hand sink placement that would cost another few hundred dollars to fix. Money was tighter than the loan officer's spreadsheet had suggested it would be, mostly because the used oven they had bought needed a part that was back-ordered three weeks. Dee had taken to sleeping on an air mattress in the back office some nights to let in early deliveries, which Nora appreciated and worried about in equal measure. They had set a soft-opening date and then quietly agreed not to tell anyone outside the family in case it slipped again. In the evenings, when the sawdust settled, the two of them sometimes sat on overturned buckets eating takeout under a bare bulb, tired and a little sunburned from carrying supplies in from the street, trading guesses about what the dining room would look like once the paint actually matched the sample.

The night before the soft opening, Dee collapsed while restocking the bar and did not get back up on her own. Nora Fitch was in the kitchen when she heard the crash of glasses and found her sister on the floor, one side of her face gone slack, unable to finish a sentence she had started normally a moment before. The ambulance took eleven minutes that felt like an hour. At the hospital, a doctor Nora had never met used the word stroke twice before Nora could make herself ask any questions, and then used the words "too soon to say" about nearly everything else that mattered. She sat in a plastic chair in a hallway that smelled of antiseptic, still wearing the apron she had on when the glasses broke, and called their mother with a voice she did not recognize as her own. The soft opening, three miles away, would go on without either of them; Nora had asked the one cook they had hired to lock up and leave the lights off. She did not think about the restaurant again that night. She sat outside a closed hospital room, watching a monitor she did not know how to read, and waited.

Ten days later, Dee could grip a pen again but not yet make it form her name, and the right side of her face still did not fully answer when she tried to smile. Nora Fitch had missed enough of the new restaurant's opening week that the distributor, unpaid twice, put their account on hold, and the part-time cook, unsupervised and unsure when Nora would return, had quietly taken a job somewhere steadier. The loan officer left a message about a missed payment and a phrase, "options going forward," that Nora understood well enough not to want to return the call. She spent her days in a hospital chair reading the same paragraph of a paperback over and over without absorbing it, and her nights on the office air mattress Dee had used before any of this happened, because going home to an empty apartment felt worse than the vinyl smell of the waiting room. The sign for the new restaurant, ordered weeks ago, arrived at the shuttered storefront with no one there to receive it, and sat propped against the locked door in its shipping crate, spelling out a name no one was left to open the doors under.

stories.title: Dead Reckoning
passages: By the time Josie Marchetti brought the biplane down in front of the grandstand, rolling gently to a stop with a wingtip nearly brushing the fence, the crowd was already on its feet. She had looped the field twice more than the program called for, unable to resist the light that afternoon, and the announcer had to shout twice before the applause let him finish her name. A man in a good suit was waiting by the hangar when she climbed down, introducing himself as a representative of the Bellweather Motor Company, and asking, before she had even pulled off her goggles, whether she had ever considered flying coast to coast. He used the word "record" twice and "sponsor" once, and mentioned a figure that made her mechanic, Walt, let out a low whistle from where he stood wiping his hands on a rag. Josie signed nothing that day, but she shook the man's hand twice, once out of manners and once because she wanted to feel, again, that it was real. That night she and Walt sat on the hangar steps long after the last car had left the field, talking through a route neither of them had flown, grinning like children.

The weeks that followed settled into a rhythm of lists. Josie Marchetti spent her mornings poring over maps with Walt, marking fuel stops across country neither of them had crossed by air, and her afternoons answering telegrams from the Bellweather office about schedules and photographs. The company sent a new compass that Walt judged to be a genuine improvement, though the replacement fuel tank they shipped arrived dented and had to be sent back, costing them a week. Weather reports for the mountain stretch were inconclusive this early in the season, neither reassuring nor alarming, so they planned around an average that might mean nothing at all. A local paper ran a small item about the upcoming attempt, respectful but brief, tucked beside the grain prices. Josie practiced dead reckoning over the county at night, since the route would demand long stretches without landmarks, and mostly trusted her figures, though twice she came in further off course than she liked. Walt kept finding small things to adjust on the engine, none of them urgent, all of them, he said, worth doing anyway before they asked it to fly that far.

Nine days before the scheduled departure, Josie Marchetti took the biplane up for what should have been a routine shakedown and brought it back down in a hay field eleven miles short of the airfield, the engine coughing and losing power in a way Walt could not diagnose just by listening. He spent two days with his head under the cowling before finding a cracked line that had likely been weakening for weeks. The part they needed was not stocked closer than three states away, and the Bellweather office, when Josie wired them, replied with a shorter message than she would have liked, noting only that the schedule "should be maintained if possible." A rival attempt, financed by a competing engine maker, was rumored to be departing from the coast within the month, and the newspaper item this time used the word "delayed" in its headline, which stung more than she expected. Walt worked past midnight twice that week without being asked. Josie caught herself, more than once, standing at the hangar door staring at a sky that seemed, for no good reason she could name, less friendly than it had a few weeks before.

The storm was not supposed to reach the mountains until evening, but Josie Marchetti flew into the leading edge of it two hours after the pass that separated her from clear country on the other side. The turbulence dropped the biplane hard enough that a strut she would have sworn was sound let go somewhere over a ridge she never saw clearly, and the last mile was less flying than falling with intention. She came down in a stand of pine that tore the wings off before the fuselage stopped, and woke sometime later unable to feel her left leg, with blood in one eye and the smell of fuel thick enough to taste. It took search parties two full days to find the wreckage, following a smoke trail from a small fire she had managed to light with a flare. By the time they carried her out on a litter down a trail no stretcher was built for, the plane behind her was little more than scattered metal and cloth going gray with rain, and the record attempt, the newspapers would say by morning, was being called a tragedy narrowly avoided rather than the disaster it had actually been.

The doctor at the county hospital told Josie Marchetti, without much softening, that the leg would heal crooked no matter what they did now, and that the vision in her left eye might return in full or might not; there was no way yet to know which. Bellweather's telegram arrived four days into her stay, thanking her for her service to the company and regretting that, under the circumstances, they would be redirecting the sponsorship toward "a candidate better positioned to succeed." A newspaper she was not supposed to have gotten hold of ran a cartoon of a woman in goggles flying blindly into a mountain, captioned with a joke about vanity, and she read it twice before a nurse took the paper away. Walt came every visiting hour without fail, but even he could not say what remained of the biplane was worth repairing, only that he had not yet had the heart to sell it for scrap. She lay in a ward that smelled of carbolic soap, her leg in traction, and could not, for the first time since she had first taken the stick of a plane as a girl, make herself imagine the sky as anything other than the thing that had tried to kill her.

By the time Josie Marchetti could walk without the cane, six months had passed and the flying community had largely moved on to talk of other attempts, other names. She took a job sweeping hangars and logging fuel receipts at the same airfield where she had once been cheered, paid barely enough to cover the room she rented in town, and most of the men who worked the field were polite to her in the careful way people are polite to someone they consider finished. Walt still had not sold the wreck, which sat under a tarp behind the third hangar collecting dust and the occasional joke from younger mechanics who did not know whose it had been. Her leg ached badly in wet weather, and some mornings the limp was worse than others for no reason she could find. One evening Walt found her staring at the tarp and said, without much preamble, that he thought there was still a good engine somewhere under all that ruined fabric, if she ever wanted to find out. She did not answer him that night, but she also did not tell him to sell it.

Through that winter, Josie Marchetti and Walt worked on the wreck in whatever hours the airfield did not need them, stripping the ruined fabric from the frame and testing what remained of the engine piece by piece in the unheated third hangar. Some parts proved sound and some did not, and there was no telling which until they had taken each one fully apart. Money for new fabric and cable came slowly, mostly from her wages and a little from Walt's, and twice they had to stop for a month until they had saved enough to keep going. Her leg had settled into a permanent, manageable stiffness that she had learned to work around, climbing the wing struts a little more carefully than she used to. Nobody at the airfield asked much about the project anymore, which suited her, since she had nothing yet worth telling them. The frame, by February, at least resembled an airplane again, primered but unpainted, sitting on wheels instead of blocks. Walt said it might fly by spring, might not, and Josie found she could hear that sentence now without either despairing or expecting too much from it.

The rebuilt plane left the ground on the first real try, in April, and Josie Marchetti flew it in a wide, careful circle over the airfield with her hands steadier than she had expected them to be. Walt watched from the ground with his arms crossed the whole time and admitted afterward, grudgingly, that he had been holding his breath. A reporter from the regional paper, tipped off by someone at the field, wrote a piece calling her return "a quieter kind of record," and this time the story ran above the fold rather than beside the grain prices. A hardware store owner who had read the article drove out to the field the following week and offered to cover fuel and parts for a modest exhibition flight, not the sum Bellweather once had, but real money offered freely. Her leg still ached climbing into the cockpit, and she still flinched, once, at a gust that reminded her too much of the mountain pass, but she did not turn back. That evening she wrote to her mother for the first time in nearly a year, not to explain anything, just to say that she was flying again, and meant to keep at it.

By early summer, Josie Marchetti had flown the rebuilt plane in three small regional meets, placing well enough in a distance event outside the county fair that a photograph of her climbing down from the cockpit ran in two papers she had never sold a story to herself. Her mother wrote back after the summer's first letter, a short note that nonetheless ended with an invitation to Sunday dinner, the first in over two years, and Josie went, sitting at a table that felt smaller than she remembered and larger than she had expected to be welcomed back to. Walt had taken to introducing her, when strangers asked, simply as "the pilot," without any qualifier attached to the word anymore. A letter arrived from a machinists' union hall proposing to underwrite a proper attempt at the transcontinental record the following autumn, modest compared to Bellweather's old terms but sincere, and signed by men who had read about the crash and the rebuilding both. Josie kept the letter on the kitchen table for three days before answering it, not out of doubt, she realized, but simply to enjoy, a little longer, the feeling of being asked rather than dropped.

Preparations for the autumn attempt went more carefully than the first ever had, Josie Marchetti and Walt double-checking fittings they would have trusted without a second look two years before. The union's money covered fuel and lodging along the route but little more, so they patched a torn aileron fabric themselves rather than order new, a repair Walt judged sound though not pretty. Weather along the mountain stretch looked ordinary for the season, not threatening, though Josie found herself reading the forecasts twice now where once she would have read them once and trusted her memory. Word came that autumn that banks in two nearby towns had shut their doors that month, and the union hall's treasurer wrote to say their remaining pledge might arrive a little late, though he did not say it would not arrive at all. Walt's cough, which he had waved off all summer as nothing, had gotten bad enough that Josie made him see a doctor, who prescribed rest that Walt mostly ignored. They set a departure date two weeks out, packed the maps in the same case as before, and tried, with only partial success, not to talk about the mountain pass by name.

Four days before the departure date, Walt did not come to the hangar, and when Josie Marchetti drove to his boarding house to find out why, the landlady met her on the porch already crying, having found him that morning in his chair, his heart simply having stopped sometime in the night. Josie sat with the undertaker's forms in her lap for an hour before she could make herself sign anything. The same week, the union hall's treasurer wrote to say that two of their contributing locals had lost their strike funds in the bank failures and could no longer honor any part of the pledge, leaving barely enough for fuel one-way. She stood in the third hangar that had been theirs for two winters, surrounded by tools she did not know how to use the way Walt had, and understood that she was expected, in four days, to fly a mountain pass that had already tried to kill her once, alone, in a plane whose engine only one man had ever fully understood, and that man was being buried on Thursday in a suit his sister had to borrow money to pay for.

Josie Marchetti took off before dawn on the day she had set months earlier, alone, with Walt's final notes on the engine folded in her jacket pocket instead of read aloud beside her the way she had always had them. She radioed a position report crossing the first range, her voice, the ground operator would say later, sounding steady enough. The second report, expected two hours after, never came. A search went out from the nearest airfield by that afternoon and continued for eleven days across a stretch of mountain forest too vast and too green to give up much to men on foot or in borrowed planes, turning up nothing that could be called wreckage, only, on the ninth day, a single strip of fabric caught high in a stand of pine that might or might not have come from her wings. The union hall paid for the search out of what remained of the pledge until the money ran out, and then it paid for a small memorial service instead, held in the same hangar where she and Walt had once rebuilt an engine together. No one at the service could say, honestly, what had happened to her, only that she had gone up, and had not come down.
